Technical reference: the cleangrowth() pipeline

2026-11-09

Source: vignettes/wrapper.Rmd
wrapper.Rmd

Purpose. This is a technical reference with an extremely detailed description of the wrapper cleangrowth(). It is primarily intended for developers, but may be of interest to people who want to know more about how growthcleanr works.

Reference structure

growthcleanr is an R package for automated data cleaning of anthropometric data. It consists of 3 main components: a child algorithm, an adult algorithm, and a function cleangrowth() that performs pre- and post-processing. Each main component has its own narrative, which provides technical detail about the algorithm and code.

This document provides a technical reference for cleangrowth() (the package’s public entry point), including the preprocessing, reference-table loading, batching, dispatch, and output-assembly infrastructure that surrounds the two algorithms. The child algorithm was developed first, and the adult algorithm was implemented in R with a different structure and integrated later. Pre-processing is not entirely consistent between the two algorithms, which is reflected in cleangrowth(). For example, some child-specific processing happens in cleangrowth(). The algorithms have different optional parameters and optional output because of different features of the algorithm and differences in implementation.

This document describes what the current R code does in the package wrapper. The two cleaning algorithms and the helper functions are documented separately:

  • vignette("child-algorithm") — child algorithm (Child Steps 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15/16, 17, 19, 21, 22)
  • vignette("adult-algorithm") — adult algorithm (Adult Steps 1, 2W, 3, 4W, 9Wa/9H/9Wb, 10H/10W, 11H/11Wa/11Wa2/11Wb, 13, 14)
  • vignette("utilities") — select pre- and post-processing helper functions (not part of the cleaning algorithms)

Child Step 2b (Gestational Age Correction) is documented here because it runs as preprocessing inside cleangrowth(), before dispatch to either algorithm.

How to Read This Document

This narrative is structured to mirror the algorithm narratives where useful. Child and adult algorithm steps are all named and numbered within the code and the reference. This wrapper reference includes named phases rather than numbered steps to describe the function of cleangrowth().

Scope and Contents

This narrative covers everything that runs in the package infrastructure:

  • The cleangrowth() public interface (input vectors, output data.table)
  • Input validation, unit conversion, LENGTHCM relabeling
  • internal_id assignment and the user-id preservation contract
  • Z-score calculation pipeline (CSD method, WHO/CDC blending, recentering, Child Step 2b GA correction)
  • Adult/child age split and dispatch to cleanchild() / cleanadult()
  • Reference-table loading, gc_preload_refs(), and checkpointed runs (checkpoint_dir); incremental re-cleans are a separate wrapper, gc_partial_run()
  • Outer-batch memory management and inner parallel batching
  • Output reassembly (combining child + adult results, NA semantics for cross-algorithm columns)
  • Wrapper-level configurable arguments
  • Cross-cutting conventions and pitfalls

The two algorithm narratives focus on what happens once a batch of pediatric or adult data is dispatched to cleanchild() or cleanadult().

Key Concepts (wrapper-level)

Data retention: Although we refer to values as being excluded, growthcleanr does not remove any values from the dataset returned to users. It adds a column to the user’s input recommending inclusion or exclusion. It does exclude values from further consideration in cleaning. For example, a value of 690 kg will be excluded early in the algorithm and is ignored thereafter. As shorthand, we refer to this process as excluding a value.

Two ways subjects are grouped — keep them distinct: internal batches are the in-memory groups cleangrowth() processes one at a time (batch_size, default 5,000 subjects) purely to cap peak memory; they are invisible in the output and do not affect results. Checkpoints are the separate subject groups that cleangrowth() splits a large dataset into and writes to disk (checkpoint_size), cleaning each with a nested cleangrowth() call. Checkpointing is on by default (checkpoint = TRUE): it engages once a dataset exceeds one checkpoint (more than checkpoint_size subjects), writing to an ephemeral per-session temp dir unless you set checkpoint_dir for a persistent, resumable location; checkpoint = FALSE turns it off entirely. Small and typical datasets stay at or below one checkpoint, so they use only internal batches and write nothing. The two groupings are independent (batch_size < checkpoint_size is allowed). (Separately, the internal checkpoint_data object mentioned later is an unrelated z-score capture, not a checkpoint.)

Three growth parameters: growthcleanr cleans weight (WEIGHTKG), height/length (HEIGHTCM/LENGTHCM), and head circumference (HEADCM). LENGTHCM is relabeled to HEIGHTCM — only the param value changes; the measurement value is not altered, i.e. no adjustment is made for the ~0.7 cm difference between recumbent length and standing height because of inconsistency in measurement and recording practices (the optional length.adjust opts into a reconciliation), except for gestational-age-corrected children between chronological age 2 and corrected age 2 (Phase 8, fact 6). Z-scores use a length-based reference <2y and a height-based reference ≥2y; the underlying source is WHO <2y, a WHO/CDC blend 2-5y, and CDC >5y. Full length/height rules are in Phase 8 (Length vs. height handling). HEADCM is cleaned through age 5 years (marked Exclude-Not-Cleaned, reported as Exclude-HC-Out-of-Range, for agedays >= 1827), because the WHO HC z-score reference ends at 5 years, so recentered z-scores cannot be formed beyond that. The recentering file provides HC rcmedian.sd through 5 years; a post-recentering safety check re-asserts Exclude-Not-Cleaned at agedays >= 1827. The adult algorithm cleans HT and WT only: adult HEADCM rows are marked Exclude-Not-Cleaned (reported as Exclude-HC-Out-of-Range) after cleanadult() returns, and adult LENGTHCM/LENGTHIN rows are relabeled HEIGHTCM/HEIGHTIN before dispatch, so adult length is cleaned as height (relabel only; length.adjust does not apply to adults).

Child-adult split: Rows are assigned to the child or adult algorithm based on row-level age. By default, rows with agedays < 20*365.25 are evaluated by the child algorithm, and rows with agedays >= 20*365.25 are evaluated by the adult algorithm. If a subject has rows that span both ages, their child and adult rows will be evaluated separately and then combined in the output.

CSD z-scores, not LMS: Z-scores for the child algorithm are calculated in the wrapper. growthcleanr z-score calculations use the Conditional Standard Deviation (CSD) method, not the standard LMS method. The CSD method uses the absolute value of half the distance between the median and +2SDs (SDpos) and the median and -2SDs (SDneg) as stand-ins for a standard deviation. The CSD z-score then equals (value - median)/SD, using SDpos for values above the median and SDneg for values below the median. The LMS method accounts for skewness in the distribution of weights, which is often useful, but in cleaning it reduces the ability of z-scores to distinguish large absolute differences in weight for heavier children, reducing cleaning accuracy. The child algorithm uses several variants of CSD z-scores (sd.orig, tbc.sd, sd.corr, ctbc.sd) — see “Z-Score Infrastructure” below. The adult algorithm does not use WHO/CDC z-scores; it works with raw measurements and BMI, plus a small embedded NHANES CSD reference used only in Evil Twins and the unit-error range.

Dual z-scores for prematurity correction: For child subjects whose data are consistent with prematurity or SGA, a corrected z-score (sd.corr) is calculated using gestational-age reference values (see Gestational-age reference values). Corrected z-scores are used as an extra check to prevent exclusion of values that are plausible for a baby with very low birth weight. See the Child Step 2b section below for the full GA-correction logic.

Recentering: After calculating CSD z-scores, the algorithm subtracts a population-level median z-score for each parameter, sex, and age to create “to-be-cleaned” SD scores (tbc.sd from sd.orig, ctbc.sd from sd.corr). Because the median z-score changes with age, using an unrecentered z-score can lead to bias in exclusions when comparing z-scores across long time periods. By default the recentering medians come from a fixed reference file (rcfile-resmoothed.csv.gz) built offline by smoothing per-day median SD scores from large electronic health record samples; see vignette("recentering") for the derivation. Recentering can instead be turned off with sd.recenter = "none" (so tbc.sd = sd.orig), or a caller-supplied sd.recenter table can be used. All feed the same recentering subtraction below.

User id is preserved and returned to the user. internal_id is the algorithm’s internal identifier used for sorting: cleangrowth() assigns internal_id as a sequential integer 1:N in id-sorted order at session start. All internal sorting and tiebreaking uses internal_id. The user’s original id column is preserved as-is into output and is never used for algorithm logic. Both algorithms share this contract.

Age-dependent internal_id tiebreaking (child): When resolving same-day duplicates, the child algorithm uses an age-dependent rule: at birth (agedays == 0), keep the lowest internal_id (earliest measurement, before postnatal fluid shifts and interventions); at all other ages, keep the highest internal_id (later measurement, which may represent a more careful re-measurement). The adult algorithm always keeps the highest internal_id.

Architecture: cleangrowth()

cleangrowth() (in child_clean.R, despite the file name) is the package’s public entry point. It accepts either a data.frame/data.table (data-frame style, primary) or six parallel input vectors (vector style, legacy backward-compatibility path) plus a long parameter list, builds a single working data.table, splits it by age into pediatric and adult strata, computes z-scores and recentering for the pediatric branch, dispatches each stratum to its specialized cleaning routine (cleanchild() / cleanadult()), and reassembles outputs in the original input row order.

The two algorithms (cleanchild(), cleanadult()) live in child_clean.R and adult_clean.R respectively. The wrapper guarantees them clean, validated, batched input and combines their results into a single output data.table.

Phase overview

cleangrowth() runs as a sequence of numbered phases. Phases 6–14 execute once per outer batch; all other phases run once per call. The numbering is not consecutive: Phase 2 no longer exists — it was a partial-run filter that has been removed (incremental re-cleans now live in the standalone gc_partial_run() wrapper; see Partial runs and preloaded references below). The remaining numbers are kept as-is so cross-references stay stable.

Phase Purpose
1 Parameter validation, NULL-binding block
3 Build data.all.ages; assign internal_id
4 Outer-batch construction (memory); load shared constants
5 Parallel cluster setup (no-op if parallel = FALSE)
6 Per-batch pediatric/adult row split
7 Imperial → metric conversion (pediatric)
8 LENGTHCM → HEIGHTCM relabel
9 Inner-batch assignment + CSD z-scores (WHO, CDC, blend)
10 GA correction for potcorr subjects (Child Step 2b)
11 Recentering; Exclude-Missing / Exclude-Not-Cleaned assignment
12 Checkpoint capture + dispatch to cleanchild()
13 Dispatch to cleanadult(); post-dispatch Exclude-Missing
14 Per-batch output reassembly (child + adult harmonization)
15 Batch teardown, bin_exclude/tri_exclude, exclusion-code remap, trim

Most phases are pre- and post-processing bookkeeping. Phases 9 and 10 (z-scores and GA correction) are the only wrapper-level phases that directly affect child algorithm behavior.

Phase-by-phase walkthrough of cleangrowth()

Phase 1: Parameter validation

cf_rescue is constrained to "standard" | "none" | "all": an explicit check first stops on TRUE/FALSE with a pointer to the 2.x include.carryforward equivalent, then match.arg() resolves the value (unambiguous abbreviations work). A long block of <- NULL assignments declares the data.table column names that will be created later; these exist purely to silence R CMD check’s “no visible binding for global variable” notes and have no runtime effect.

Quality checks run shortly afterward (after the data.table is built): adult_cutpoint must be numeric and is clamped to [18, 20] (with a warning when a value is moved); adult_scale_max_lbs must be a single positive number (or Inf for no scale cap); ewma_window must be a single finite number >= 1; batch_size must be a single positive whole number; adult_overrides, if given, must be a named list whose names are recognized adult settings (each value’s type is checked against the preset it replaces when the adult algorithm runs); rows whose param (after param_coding resolution) is not one of the accepted parameter strings are set aside at entry (with their original measurement preserved — gc must not mutate the user’s data; contributes an “unrecognized parameters” bullet to the consolidated input warning, below) into a notgc_rows holdout, never enter z-score calculation or cleaning, and are rebound after the batch loop with the internal code Exclude-Not-GC-Param (see Phase 15).

A character measurement is converted to numbers, with a message; text that is not a number becomes missing and is set aside as Exclude-Missing-Info. A factor measurement is converted through its labels (never its level codes), with a warning, and then handled the same way.

agedays given as a time difference (difftime, for example from subtracting dates or date-times) is converted to days in its own units, with a warning when the units are not days, so a difference in hours is not read as days. A factor agedays is converted through its labels with a warning, and character agedays is converted to numbers; values that are not numbers are set aside. Output agedays is returned as submitted.

Phase 2: removed (former partial-run filter)

Phase 2 was a partial-run filter that sliced the input down to changed subjects when a cache was supplied. It has been removed: incremental re-cleans are now handled entirely outside cleangrowth() by the standalone gc_partial_run() wrapper, which slices to the changed subjects, calls cleangrowth() on that subset like any other input, and merges the cached rows back at the output level. See Partial runs and preloaded references in the Batching and Dispatch section. The phase number is retained (not reused) so the later phase numbers stay stable.

Phase 3: data.table construction and internal_id assignment

The five input vectors plus a line index (the original input row position, which is what the output will eventually be re-sorted to) are bound into data.all.ages. Two measurement columns are stored: v is the metric-target value with 0 → NaN applied (used by the child algorithm), and v_adult is the original measurement preserved in its caller-supplied units (used by cleanadult(), which performs its own imperial conversion). subjid, sex, and param are each stored twice: the interpreted/working value (subjid as a factor, sex, param) drives the algorithm, and the verbatim submission (subjid_input, sex_input, param_input) is preserved for output fidelity and restored as the primary output column at the Phase 15 trim (so a numeric subjid is returned numeric, not as a factor). sex is recoded to 0L/1L/NA and param to a canonical parameter token per the flexible-coding rules — see Flexible sex and parameter coding under Data Requirements for the accepted codings, the sex_coding / param_coding overrides, the 1=male/2=female hard stop, and the unrecognized-value handling. Both recodings run just before this construction.

id is optional. At entry the wrapper snapshots the user-supplied id as user_id_orig and validates it: absent / NULL / NA / non-unique → id is replaced with seq_along(measurement) (sequential 1:N in input row order) for all internal use and a Generated ids section is added to the consolidated input warning (below). Valid id is used as-is. A length mismatch between id and measurement is still a hard stop() (no sensible recovery). id (now guaranteed unique) is stored on data.all.ages. The table is then keyed by (subjid, param, agedays, id) and internal_id := seq_len(.N) is assigned. internal_id is the sequential integer used for all internal sorting and tiebreaking; the (possibly regenerated) id is the wrapper-level sort key. user_id_orig is restored to the output id column at Phase 15 trim (when a regen occurred); the gc-used id is surfaced as the optional gc_internal_id output column when display_gc_id = TRUE or full_detail = TRUE.

Consolidated input warning

The input checks above do not each raise their own warning(). Instead they accumulate headlined bullets and cleangrowth() emits a single warning() after input validation, with up to two capped sections:

  • Unusable data — rows growthcleanr could not use, each as one bullet with a short headline, an N and %, an example subjid, what gc did, and a suggested fix. It leads with a summary line reporting the union of distinct set-aside rows (N of M measurement(s) (X%) could not be used as submitted and were set aside), so a row failing two checks is not double-counted, and frames the situation as commonly expected. Bullets: blank required fields (NA in subjid/param/agedays/measurement); unrecognized parameters (leads with param_coding); unrecognized/blank pediatric sex (leads with sex_coding); and three value-defect bullets — zero measurement, negative measurement, and negative agedays — reported neutrally (some are expected in EHR extracts), with per-parameter-group N/% for the two measurement problems and all-rows N/% for age.
  • Generated ids — present only when id was absent / NA / non-unique and gc auto-generated 1:N; it states what happened and explains that the id drives deterministic tie-breaking among equally-plausible measurements (prefers the higher id, except lowest at birth), so supplying your own gives reproducibility and control. The notice for an absent id is shown once per R session (it would otherwise repeat identically for every call in a loop; a gc_runtrial() trial reports it without using it up for the full run); notices for NA or duplicated id values describe the dataset and are shown every run.

Class-1 interpretation-mismatch bullets (unrecognized sex/param) lead with the growthcleanr-argument fix rather than telling the user to edit their data; Class-2 defect bullets (blank, zero, negative) report scope only. Hard stops (the 1=male/2=female trap; no pediatric row with a usable sex) remain immediate stop()s and are not buffered.

Cleaning summary

Unless quietly = TRUE, cleangrowth() also prints a short cleaning summary via message() — a ****-bounded headline of what it did. Per metric parameter group, reported weight first, then height, then head circumference, it gives the count and percentage included (kept as Include) versus excluded (flagged implausible by the algorithm), then an overall set aside count (rows unusable as submitted, which were never cleaned — the same rows the Unusable data warning details), and, only when some rows have no result (a resumed checkpoint run whose input changed), a no result count. A nonzero percentage below 0.05% is shown as <0.1%. Per-parameter percentages are of that parameter’s included + excluded total (the rows that were cleaned); the “set aside” percentage is of all submitted measurements. It is built by .gc_cleaning_summary_lines() from the final exclude column, so it reflects the actual result.

The cleaning summary prints at the minimal (default) and verbose levels but is suppressed by quietly = TRUE (which turns off progress lines and the summary; warnings still appear); you can also silence just this line with suppressMessages() if you are running gc in a loop. It is emitted once per run — for a checkpointed run, the outer call prints it and the per-checkpoint calls stay silent.

The Unusable data / Generated ids bullets are built by the detector .gc_detect_setaside() (in R/child_clean.R), which runs once over the whole input and returns the bullet text without changing any row. It does not assign the exclusion codes — those come from a separate mechanism: unrecognized-parameter and missing-subjid/param rows are set aside inline during preprocessing (Exclude-Not-GC-Param / Exclude-Missing), and the other categories (blank / zero / negative measurement, negative agedays, unrecognized pediatric sex) become Exclude-Missing-Info when the cleaning algorithm processes their NA/NaN values. These two paths describe the same rows and must stay in agreement: every category the warning reports as set aside must be a category the code path actually excludes, with the same membership rule — a change to one (a new set-aside reason, a shifted threshold, a redefined category) requires the matching change to the other, or the count a user sees in the warning will not match the codes in the output. The checkpoint path relies on this too: it runs the detector once in the outer call (see Checkpointed runs, below) while the per-checkpoint calls assign the codes, so the two only agree because they apply the same rules to the same rows.

Phase 4: Outer-batch construction and shared constants

Subjects (not rows) are partitioned into outer batches of batch_size (default 5000); the batches data.table maps subjid → batch. Each outer-batch iteration operates on a fresh data.all / data.adult / data.batch copy that gets garbage-collected before the next iteration, which limits the memory the cleaning steps use; the full input and the combined result are still held in memory. The inner parallel batching (Phase 9) is layered on top.

Two batch-invariant constants are also built here: the exclude.levels factor (concatenation of exclude.levels.peds and exclude.levels.adult, used everywhere the exclude factor is constructed) and the Tanner height-velocity reference (loaded once from inst/extdata/tanner_ht_vel.csv.gz, used by Child Step 17 of cleanchild()). The Tanner table is loaded even for all-adult datasets — the cost is negligible (~0.01 s).

Phase 5: Parallel cluster setup

When parallel = TRUE and the resolved worker count cores > 1, a single makeCluster(cores) is created here and torn down once after the outer loop (Phase 15). All algorithm-internal functions are exported via clusterExport() — both child (.child_valid, ewma, read_anthro, as_matrix_delta, identify_temp_sde, get_dop, calc_otl_evil_twins, calc_and_recenter_z_scores, .child_exc, ewma_cache_init / update) and adult (cleanadult, permissiveness_presets, resolve_permissiveness, compute_et_limit, compute_perc_limit, compute_wtallow, evil_twins, propagate_to_rv, remove_ewma_wt, remove_mod_ewma_wt, eval_2d_nonord, eval_1d, eval_error_load, etc.). cores (the worker/split count) resolves to min(8, detectCores() - 1) when parallel = TRUE and cores = NULL; a user-supplied cores is used, capped (with a warning) at the detected core count. When parallel = FALSE (or the resolved count is 1) no cluster is built. The cost of cluster creation is amortized across all outer batches. In a checkpointed run, each checkpoint is its own nested call and creates its own cluster, so this saving applies within a checkpoint.

Phase 6: Outer-batch loop — pediatric/adult split

For each outer batch id_batch, three working copies are made from data.all.ages:

  • data.all — pediatric rows (agedays < adult_cutpoint * 365.25)
  • data.adult — adult rows (agedays >= adult_cutpoint * 365.25)
  • data.batch — all rows for this batch’s subjects (used for output assembly)

The split is row-level, not subject-level: a subject who has measurements before and after the cutpoint will appear in both data.all and data.adult. There is no cross-stratum logic — each side is processed independently and their results are concatenated in Phase 14. If either side is empty, the corresponding processing block is skipped and an empty data.table is used as the placeholder.

Rows with agedays = NA fall through both comparisons (NA < cutpoint and NA >= cutpoint both evaluate to NA, not TRUE) and enter neither data.all nor data.adult. They are carried into data.batch and receive Exclude-Missing during Phase 14 reassembly.

Phase 7: Imperial → metric conversion (pediatric only)

Before z-score calculation, data.all is converted in place: HEIGHTIN → HEIGHTCM (v := v * 2.54), LENGTHIN → LENGTHCM (v := v * 2.54), HEADIN → HEADCM (v := v * 2.54), and WEIGHTLBS → WEIGHTKG (v := v / 2.2046226). The param strings are then overwritten with the metric labels (a LENGTHIN becomes LENGTHCM and rides the length path from there). The adult algorithm performs its own conversion internally on v_adult, which is why v_adult is preserved unchanged on data.all.ages.

Phase 8: Length vs. height handling (LENGTHCM → HEIGHTCM relabel and length.adjust)

This section is the single source of truth for how growthcleanr handles recumbent length vs standing height. The rules below are six distinct facts; they are easy to conflate, so every other mention in the documentation points here instead of restating them.

1. Relabel (label only). Every LENGTHCM row is internally relabeled HEIGHTCM here, so all downstream pediatric logic treats a single linear parameter. Only the internal param label changes — the measurement value is not touched by the relabel. (Imperial LENGTHIN was already converted to LENGTHCM in Phase 7 and rides this path from there.) The output param column returns the submitted label verbatim; the internal relabel is surfaced only in the optional gc_internal_param column.

2. The reference is chosen by age — not by the label, and not by length.adjust. The WHO/CDC linear reference is length-based under 2 years and height-based at 2 years and older. The source is WHO under 2 years, a WHO/CDC blend from 2 to 5 years, and CDC over 5 years. In growthcleanr, “2 years” for length vs height means day 730: the reference files switch from length to height values at agedays 730, and every length/height decision below uses the same day (.gc_ht_start_day). The one intentional exception is the Child Step 17 WHO velocity check, whose range runs through 24 months (730.5 days), so a pair of heights ending at day 730 is still checked against the WHO increments. This age-based selection is built into the age-indexed reference itself: it does not depend on whether a value was submitted as LENGTHCM or HEIGHTCM, and it is not changed by length.adjust.

3. By default, no recumbent-vs-standing adjustment is made. Recumbent length runs about 0.7 cm longer than standing height for the same child, but by default growthcleanr does not adjust the measurement for this offset, because measurement and recording practices for length vs height vary widely across health systems and are rarely reliable in extracted EHR data. All linear measurements under 2 years are evaluated as length and all at 2 years and older as height, against the age-based reference in fact 2. The one exception is gestational-age-corrected children between chronological age 2 and corrected age 2 (fact 6).

4. length.adjust = TRUE optionally reconciles the offset, in both directions. It reconciles how a value was entered with what the reference at that age expects:

Entered as Age Adjustment Example
LENGTHCM 2 years or older (day 730 on) −0.7 cm 92 cm at 30 months is z-scored as 91.3
HEIGHTCM under 2 years (before day 730) +0.7 cm 74 cm at 21 months is z-scored as 74.7
LENGTHCM under 2 years (before day 730) none recumbent is what the reference expects
HEIGHTCM 2 years or older (day 730 on) none standing is what the reference expects

The cutoff is agedays >= 730, the day the reference files switch to height, so the two directions partition cleanly and every linear row is offset at most once. Rows with a missing agedays are left alone. The adjustment runs after the imperial→metric conversion (Phase 7) and before the relabel (fact 1); the offset is applied only where a value is z-scored (the uncorrected and corrected z-scores and their plus/minus perturbations). The measurement value itself is not changed: the checks that work in raw centimeters (carried-forward and same-day identical detection, the velocity check in Child Step 17, the centimeter hard limits, and the unit-error range) use the entered value, so a value repeated across the 2-year boundary is still recognized as repeated. The returned measurement is the verbatim submission, and gc_internal_meas (internal_detail = TRUE) is the entered value in metric units, without the offset. It is pediatric-only: rows at or above adult_cutpoint are not adjusted (the adult algorithm works from raw measurements). Adult LENGTHCM/LENGTHIN rows are relabeled HEIGHTCM/HEIGHTIN (label only), so adult length is cleaned as height.

5. Semi-wide and wide input support default handling only. Because the recumbent/standing label must be carried per measurement, length.adjust is a long-format-only feature: it is rejected for input_format = "semi_wide" and "wide". In those formats a LENGTHCM/LENGTHIN value at any age gets default handling, the same as in long input with length.adjust = FALSE; submit long input for the fact-4 reconciliation.

6. Gestational-age-corrected children between chronological age 2 and corrected age 2. For a subject whose gestational-age correction applies (Child Step 2b; not reverted by the corroboration check), a height row with chronological age ≥ 2 years and corrected age < 2 years (the “GA window”; on whole days, agedays >= 730 and cagedays < 730) is scored against two references that expect different measurement methods: the uncorrected z-score (sd.orig, chronological age) against the standing-height reference, and the corrected z-score (corrected age) against the recumbent-length reference. growthcleanr uses one offset, 0.7 cm, for both references and for length.adjust.

  • Default (length.adjust = FALSE): the measurement method is presumed to follow corrected age. Most clinicians evaluate these children on length-for-age at corrected age, and many measure recumbent length after 2 years regardless, so a window value is presumed recumbent. The uncorrected z-score (and its plus/minus perturbations) uses the value minus 0.7 cm; the corrected z-score uses the value as entered. As in fact 4, the offset is applied only to z-scores: the raw-centimeter checks and gc_internal_meas use the entered value.
  • length.adjust = TRUE: the label decides. A LENGTHCM row loses 0.7 cm (fact 4) for the uncorrected z-score, and the corrected z-score uses the value as entered. A HEIGHTCM row uses the value as entered for the uncorrected z-score and adds 0.7 cm for the corrected z-score.
Setting Row Value for the uncorrected z (sd.orig) Value for the corrected z
default GA-window height row (any label) entered − 0.7 entered
length.adjust = TRUE LENGTHCM in the GA window entered − 0.7 entered
length.adjust = TRUE HEIGHTCM in the GA window entered entered + 0.7

Put simply, the default infers the measurement method from corrected age, and length.adjust = TRUE reads it from the label; a default window row is handled exactly like a length.adjust = TRUE row labeled LENGTHCM. Term children, and subjects whose correction is withdrawn, are handled by facts 3 and 4 alone. The plus/minus perturbed scores follow the same values (±1 cm).

The 0.7 cm offset follows the WHO value; the CDC methods report uses 0.8 cm, and growthcleanr uses 0.7 cm for both references so that the offset is applied consistently:

WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study Group. WHO Child Growth Standards: Length/height-for-age, weight-for-age, weight-for-length, weight-for-height and body mass index-for-age: Methods and development. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2006.

Kuczmarski RJ, Ogden CL, Guo SS, et al. 2000 CDC growth charts for the United States: Methods and development. National Center for Health Statistics. Vital Health Stat 11(246). 2002. PDF

Phase 9: Inner-batch assignment and z-score calculation

data.all is keyed by subjid, then a per-subject batch column is added ((seq_along(unique(subjid)) - 1L) %% cores + 1L). When cores > 1 this drives the foreach dispatch later; when cores == 1 it is a no-op.

Z-score calculation uses WHO and CDC reference closures from read_anthro(). If ref_tables was supplied via gc_preload_refs(), the preloaded closures are used and the disk read is skipped (~0.9 s saved per call); otherwise read_anthro() is invoked twice (once with cdc.only = TRUE, once with cdc.only = FALSE). Each closure is applied to (param, agedays, sex, v + lin_off, TRUE) to populate sd.orig_cdc and sd.orig_who, where lin_off is the z-score-only length/height offset (Phase 8). The age-blending logic writes the final sd.orig. The GA correction writes a separate sd.corr; the one exception is height rows in the gestational-age window under the default, whose sd.orig Child Step 2b rescores 0.7 cm lower (Phase 8, fact 6). sd.orig is the uncorrected score used by CF rescue and PIV. Full CSD and blending formulas are in the Z-Score Infrastructure section.

Naming quirk: sd.orig_who actually holds CDC values for ages ≥ 5y — the WHO closure falls back to CDC where WHO data is unavailable (the name is historical). This is harmless because the blending logic gives WHO zero weight at age 5+, so the CDC values sitting in sd.orig_who are never used as if they were WHO.

Phase 10: GA correction (Child Step 2b)

Subjects whose first weight is < -2 SD at < 10 months are flagged potcorr and re-scored against gestational-age reference values using postmenstrual age; the corrected z-score (sd.corr) acts as an extra check against inappropriate exclusion for plausibly-preterm infants. If no subjects qualify, the block short-circuits and skips reading the gestational-age reference files, assigning sd.corr := sd.orig and uncorr := 0L. The result columns (sd.corr, uncorr, potcorr, plus sd.corr_plus/sd.corr_minus; for default GA-window height rows also lin_off, p_plus/p_minus and the rescored sd.orig) are merged back onto data.all by internal_id; data.all is then trimmed to its original column set plus the new columns. Full mechanics (potcorr_wt flagging, two reference merges, CSD z-score formula, corrected/blended sd.c, corroboration-gated revert rule) are in the Gestational Age Correction (Child Step 2b, preprocessing) section.

Phase 11: Recentering and Missing/Not-Cleaned assignment

data.all is rekeyed (subjid, param, agedays, internal_id), and a fresh row index index := 1:.N is added. The exclude factor column is created with two pre-step assignments:

  • Exclude-Missing for is.na(v) | is.na(agedays) | agedays < 0 | v < 0 (the v < 0 term routes negative measurements to missing; the is.na(agedays) guard is defensive — NA agedays rows are normally excluded by the Phase 6 split and handled in Phase 14, but this guard catches them if they somehow reach the child path)
  • Exclude-Not-Cleaned for param == "HEADCM" & agedays >= 1827

cf_rescued is initialized to "" (Child Step 6 populates it). Recentering uses the median table selected by sd.recenter: the built-in rcfile-resmoothed.csv.gz (default, NA), an all-zero table when sd.recenter = "none" (so tbc.sd = sd.orig), or a user-supplied table (its coverage of every evaluable child row was checked before batching). It joins on (param, sex, agedays) and computes tbc.sd := sd.orig - rcmedian.sd and ctbc.sd := sd.corr - rcmedian.sd; the table is then rekeyed to (subjid, param, agedays, internal_id). Two safety checks follow: rows where tbc.sd is NA (recentering miss) get Exclude-Missing, and HC rows with agedays >= 1827 get Exclude-Not-Cleaned. The second re-assert matters because the WHO HC z-score reference (and thus tbc.sd) is NA past 5 years, so the is.na(tbc.sd) check would otherwise relabel HC > 5y as Exclude-Missing; combined with the pre-recentering agedays >= 1827 → Exclude-Not-Cleaned assignment, this keeps a single consistent Exclude-Not-Cleaned code for all HC > 5y. Recentering rationale is in the Z-Score Infrastructure section; how the packaged medians were derived is in vignette("recentering").

Phase 12: Checkpoint capture and dispatch to cleanchild()

Before dispatch, checkpoint_data is captured: a copy of (id, subjid, param, agedays, sd.orig, sd.corr, tbc.sd, ctbc.sd, rcmedian.sd, tbc.p_plus, tbc.p_minus, ctbc.p_plus, ctbc.p_minus) columns that exist on data.all (the list is intersected with the actual columns, so any not present are silently dropped). These are merged back onto the output by id after dispatch, so the user can inspect intermediate z-scores even though cleanchild() only returns (id, exclude, cf_rescued, ...); tbc.sd/ctbc.sd/rcmedian.sd are the columns surfaced by the recenter_detail output contract (a subset also surfaced by debug). (This internal checkpoint_data capture is unrelated to the public cleangrowth_checkpoint() function, which saves per-checkpoint result files to disk; see Checkpointed runs under Batching and Dispatch.)

Dispatch follows the cores switch: cores == 1 calls cleanchild() once on data.all; cores > 1 splits data.all by batch and runs cleanchild() on each piece via foreach::foreach(...) %dopar%, then rbindlist()s the per-batch results. Both paths pass the same parameters — among them the PIV cutoffs (six piv.z.*), cf_rescue, cf_detail, error.load.*, ewma_window, the output-detail flags, the preloaded Tanner table, the WHO/CDC measurement.to.z closure, and ref_tables (for any internal z-score recomputation inside cleanchild()). The result is ret.df. See Batching and Dispatch for inner-batch and parallel mechanics.

Phase 13: Adult dispatch to cleanadult()

data.adult gets its own inner-batch column (newbatch) and an age_years column, and its LENGTHCM/LENGTHIN rows are relabeled HEIGHTCM/HEIGHTIN so adult length is cleaned as height (relabel only; length.adjust does not apply to adults; the submitted label is restored at output). measurement := v_adult is set so cleanadult() reads from the original-units column (it does its own imperial conversion). Dispatch mirrors the child path: serial → single cleanadult() call; multi-batch → split(data.adult, by = "newbatch") fed through foreach::foreach(...) %dopar%/%do% and recombined with rbindlist(). adult_permissiveness, adult_scale_max_lbs, ewma_window, and adult_overrides are spliced into the cleanadult() call (adult_overrides via do.call); all other adult settings fall back to the permissiveness preset unless named in adult_overrides.

After cleanadult() returns, Exclude-Missing is applied post-dispatch (res[is.na(measurement) | agedays < 0 | measurement < 0, result := "Exclude-Missing"]), which is where negative measurements and negative ages are also set aside. This differs from the child path, where Exclude-Missing is set before dispatch (because .child_valid() needs it pre-set to filter rows). Missing measurements (NA/NaN) do not rely on this post-dispatch pass, however: cleanadult() sets any row with a missing measurement aside as Exclude-Missing at entry and drops it from the per-subject height/weight working sets, so it never participates in a step or feeds a derived quantity (BMI, EWMA, median). The post-dispatch assignment then re-asserts the same code on those rows (idempotent) and additionally covers the negative-value cases. Finally, adult head-circumference rows (HEADCM/HEADIN), which cleanadult() never reads, are set to Exclude-Not-Cleaned (reported as Exclude-HC-Out-of-Range).

cleanadult() interface contract

Input columns (in the data.table the wrapper passes to cleanadult()): id, internal_id, subjid, sex, agedays, param, measurement. internal_id is the sequential integer key created by cleangrowth() (Phase 3); the adult algorithm uses it for deterministic sorting and named-vector indexing throughout (via as.character() for names and as.integer() for join keys). param may be HEIGHTCM / HEIGHTIN / WEIGHTKG / WEIGHTLBS — cleanadult() performs its own imperial-to-metric conversion (it reads measurement := v_adult, the original caller-supplied units). sex may be NA; when present it is used in Evil Twins and the unit-error range.

Output columns appended to the returned data.table:

  • result — adult exclusion code ("Include" or "Exclude-A-*"; see vignette("exclusion-codes")). Mapped to exclude in the combined wrapper output (Phase 14).
  • mean_ht — subject mean height (computed in Adult Step 11H). The mean_ht column can be used by researchers who want a consistent height for evaluation of body mass index.
  • bin_result (default ON) — "Include" / "Exclude" binary collapse of result.
  • extraneous, loss_groups, gain_groups — adult algorithm working columns, returned only when their corresponding emit flags are set on the cleanadult() call.

The user’s original id is preserved untouched throughout. Internal working columns (meas_m, ageyears, age_days) are dropped before return.

Phase 14: Output reassembly

ret.df (child) and res (adult) are concatenated into full_out keyed by line, with column harmonization: cf_rescued is empty string for adult rows; mean_ht and bin_result are NA for child rows. If cf_detail = TRUE, the detail columns are added: adult rows get cf_status = "Adult" and NA in the other detail columns.

full_out is then merged onto data.batch by line (preserving all original input columns), then back-merged with checkpoint_data by id (adult rows get NA for the checkpoint columns). Before reordering, any row with NA in the exclude column is assigned Exclude-Missing: these are rows present in data.batch but absent from full_out, which occurs when agedays = NA causes a row to fall through both sides of the Phase 6 split. The result is reordered to match data.batch$id (input row order for this batch) and setorder(all_results, line) restores the original input row order. The batch result is appended to results_list.

A safety guard (which actually runs post-loop — see Phase 15) catches any Exclude-C-Temp-Same-Day surviving to the final output: it issues a warning() and reclassifies the offending rows to Exclude-C-Extraneous (which then maps to Exclude-Extraneous at output). That code is internal to Child Steps 5/13 and must be resolved before assembly. The adult algorithm handles temp SDEs differently: it uses an internal extraneous boolean column on its working dataframe (set by temp_sde() in adult_support.R, consumed and resolved inside Adult Steps 9H/10W) rather than an Exclude-A-Temp-Same-Day factor code. Adult output therefore never carries a temp-SDE exclusion code, and the safety guard is specific to the child path.

Phase 15: Outer-batch teardown, bin/tri exclude, remap, and trim

After the outer loop, the parallel cluster (if any) is stopped, and results_list is rbindlist-ed with use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE (handles missing cf_status / cf_deltaz columns when cf_detail = FALSE). One more setorder(all_results, line) restores the input row order. The notgc_rows holdout set aside at entry (Phase 1) is then rebound here — measurement intact, factor code Exclude-Not-GC-Param — and the table re-setorder-ed by line.

Two derived columns are then added:

  • bin_exclude: "Include" vs "Exclude" (always present)
  • tri_exclude (opt-in via tri_exclude = TRUE): "Include" vs "Same-Day" (for any Exclude-{C,A}-Identical or Exclude-{C,A}-Extraneous) vs "Exclude" (all other Exclude values)

Exclusion-code remap (internal → Summary/Detailed). Up to this point the exclude column holds the algorithm’s internal literal codes (child Exclude-C-*, adult Exclude-A-*, plus the preprocessing Exclude-Missing / Exclude-Not-Cleaned / Exclude-Not-GC-Param). Just before the trim, a mapping layer translates these via two named-vector crosswalks defined in cleangrowth() (exclude.map.summary, exclude.map.detailed): exclude is overwritten with the Summary code (factor levels exclude.levels.summary) always, and an exclude_detailed column with the Detailed code (factor levels exclude.levels.detailed) is added when exclude_detail = TRUE (or full_detail = TRUE). The remap is idempotent — already-mapped values pass through unchanged. The internal literals are not changed anywhere in the algorithm; only this output column is remapped. Full catalog + crosswalk: vignette("exclusion-codes").

Before the trim — and, in the code, just before the exclusion-code remap described in the previous paragraph (the two are independent; both run before the trim) — the id-restoration / gc_internal_id-capture runs: if display_gc_id (or full_detail) is on, gc_internal_id := id is added (capturing the id gc used internally — i.e., the auto-regen 1:N when a regen happened, else the user’s untouched id); then, only when a regen actually replaced a user-supplied id (id_was_regened == TRUE), id := user_id_orig restores the user’s original. The positional assignment is valid because all_results is in input row order (restored by setorder(all_results, line) above) and user_id_orig is in input row order too. Then all_results is trimmed to the public column set: id, subjid, param, agedays, sex, measurement (the verbatim submitted value — v is restored to v_adult just before the trim, so the returned value is the user’s original, not the metric/0→NaN working value), exclude (Summary), bin_exclude, plus exclude_detailed, tri_exclude, cf_status/cf_deltaz, corr_val/corr_pt, unit_error_range, the recenter_detail columns (tbc.sd/ctbc.sd/rcmedian.sd), the debug z-score column set, and/or gc_internal_id when their parameters are set (the final column select is deduped, so debug + recenter_detail together do not double-list tbc.sd/ctbc.sd). All internal working columns (line, sd.orig*, tbc.sd, ctbc.sd, cf_rescued, bin_result, checkpoint columns) are dropped here. The trimmed all_results is returned. See Output Format for the column contract.

Returning the user’s input

One rule runs through the whole wrapper: a column with the user’s name holds only the user’s own values, exactly as entered. growthcleanr works on interpreted copies of the input, but what it returns under the user’s names is what the user submitted. The column-by-column contract for users is in vignette("output") (§1, “Output fidelity”, and the carry_through row); this section lists where the code applies the rule, so that a new output column or a new code path can follow it everywhere.

  • Values come back as entered. sex, param and subjid keep verbatim copies (sex_input, param_input, subjid_input) beside their working versions (Phase 3); measurement keeps v_adult (and meas_input for a text or factor column, so the submitted type is kept); and agedays keeps agedays_input beside the whole-day working value. The verbatim copies are restored just before the Phase 15 trim. growthcleanr’s interpreted values are returned only under growthcleanr names (gc_internal_*), never under the user’s.
  • Columns come back under the user’s names. After the trim, the six role columns are renamed from the canonical names to the names the user supplied (data-frame style) or that were derived from the call (vector style).
  • A user column is renamed only when it would collide. A user column (a carried column, or the user’s id in long output from semi-wide/wide input) is returned as userinput_<name>, with a warning, only when its name matches a column growthcleanr returns in this run. The list of returned columns comes from .gc_added_output_cols(), the same list that builds the Phase 15 trim, and .gc_userinput_names() applies the rename; a name growthcleanr does not return in this run is left alone.
  • Carried columns are reattached by input row position. With carry_through = TRUE, non-role columns are parked at entry in input row order and added back after the rename, by row position rather than by a join key, so no internal column (such as line) can collide with a user’s column name. The single-run path uses the input row positions captured before the trim; the checkpointed path relies on the combined result being in input row order.
  • Long output from semi-wide/wide input. .gc_crossformat_id_cols() returns the user’s id under the user’s own name (repeated on each measurement from its input row), growthcleanr’s per-measurement number as gc_internal_id, and the user’s other columns repeated from their row, with the same userinput_<name> rule.
  • Checkpointed runs follow the same steps. The checkpoint path (see Checkpointed runs) repeats the rename, carry reattachment, cross-format id handling and re-widening on the combined result, in the same order as a single run, so a checkpointed run returns the same columns and values as a single run.

Date parsing (dob + visit_date → agedays)

growthcleanr computes agedays as floor(visit_date - dob) in whole days on the date route — no agedays column, or age_source = "dates", with both dob and visit_date supplied. When agedays is supplied directly it drives the algorithm and the dates do not; but any dob and/or visit_date column that is present is still parsed so its interpretation can be returned as gc_internal_dob / gc_internal_visit_date (under internal_detail). A single date column (e.g. visit_date alone) is allowed alongside an agedays column purely for this parse-and-return; computing agedays from dates still requires both. The submitted date columns also ride through carry-through and are echoed back verbatim under their own names, so output can carry both the verbatim value and gc’s parsed Date. Parsing is shared with the semi-wide and wide adapters through the internal helpers in R/reshape_adapters.R (.gc_date_class() + .gc_parse_date_col()), so all input shapes accept the same formats.

Accepted formats fall into three pattern classes:

Class Examples date_order needed?
Year-first numeric 2013-03-04, 2013/03/04, 2013.03.04, 20130304 no
English spelled-month 03mar2013, 15-Mar-2024, March 15, 2024, 15 March 2024 no
Numeric day/month 3/4/2013, 03-04-2013 yes ("dmy" or "mdy")

Guarantees, all aimed at never silently misparsing a date:

  • Never guess order. Numeric day/month dates are ambiguous, so they are accepted only when date_order declares the order; classification is by pattern, so even a content-unambiguous value like 25/12/2013 errors without date_order. growthcleanr does not auto-detect order.
  • One format per run. All non-blank values across both dob and visit_date must resolve to a single class (separators are interchangeable within the year-first class); a mixed column errors.
  • Four-digit years only, 1900–2099. Every value must carry a 19xx/20xx year; two-digit years are rejected (the guard also blocks lubridate’s silent two-digit-year pivot).
  • English locale pinned. Spelled-month recognition uses the C (English) locale, so behavior is identical on every machine; non-English month names are rejected.
  • Blank/NA → missing agedays (downstream Exclude-Missing-Info); a numeric (epoch-integer) date column is rejected with a targeted message.
  • Text with no digits is blank. A value such as "NA", "N/A", "NULL", "." or "unknown" cannot be misread as a date, so it is treated as blank: the row gets a missing agedays and is set aside, and the input warning reports it (“Dates with no digits”).
  • A few unreadable dates are set aside. A value that matches the run’s format but is not a real date (for example "2013-02-30") is set aside the same way when there are only a few of them in a column (at most 1, or 5% of its non-blank values), and reported (“Unreadable dates”). More than that usually means the dates are not in the expected format (for example a wrong date_order), so the run stops and names examples.

The resolved dates are surfaced as the optional gc_internal_dob / gc_internal_visit_date Date columns under internal_detail / full_detail whenever the corresponding column was supplied — on the date route or alongside an agedays column — so the interpretation (including the four-digit year lubridate resolved) is auditable. Each is independent: a lone visit_date adds only gc_internal_visit_date. Parsing uses lubridate::parse_date_time(); spelled-month values are parsed by trying dmy and mdy singly and combining (a single multi-order call mis-trains on a mixed vector).

Batching and Dispatch

Purpose

The outer batching wrapper (added by Chris Penney) divides subjects into groups for memory management. Without batching, preprocessing (z-score calculation, recentering, reference table merges) for the full dataset must fit in memory at once. For large datasets (100s of thousands or millions of subjects), this can cause memory pressure. The wrapper processes one batch at a time, then combines results.

Subject-level batching

Batching occurs at the subject level, not the row level. All of a given subject’s rows — across all parameters (WEIGHTKG, HEIGHTCM, HEADCM) and all ages — are assigned to the same batch. This is a logistical choice: batching by subject before the child/adult age split keeps both halves of a subject’s data within the same outer-batch iteration, so output reassembly can combine child and adult results for that subject without cross-batch bookkeeping. The child and adult algorithms themselves are independent and do not share trajectory data across the age split.

Interaction with the child/adult age split

After batching by subject, cleangrowth() splits each batch’s data by adult_cutpoint (default 20 years, range 18–20) into pediatric (data.all) and adult (data.adult) subsets. A subject whose rows span the cutpoint will have some rows sent to cleanchild() and others to cleanadult(). This is intentional: the child and adult algorithms are independent pipelines with no interaction between them. A subject’s child measurements are cleaned using only their other child measurements, and their adult measurements are cleaned using only their other adult measurements.

Both sets of rows for such a subject are guaranteed to be in the same batch because batching is done on subjid before the age split. The result assembly at the end of each batch iteration recombines the child and adult results for the batch’s subjects, and rbindlist() combines across batches.

Two batching systems in the code

The code contains two layered batching systems with different purposes:

System 1 — Outer wrapper (for memory management):

  • In child_clean.R, inside cleangrowth().
  • Creates batches of up to batch_size subjects (default 5000; configurable via the batch_size parameter): patients[, batch := (seq_len(.N) - 1L) %/% batch_size + 1L].
  • Iterates the batches with a for loop. Each iteration filters the input to the current batch’s subjid values (both the pediatric data.all and the adult data.adult are limited to those subjects), runs preprocessing and the child/adult algorithms on just that batch, and pushes the per-batch result onto results_list.
  • After the loop, rbindlist(results_list) combines per-batch results and the merge against data.batch restores user input columns.

System 2 — Inner batching (for parallelism):

  • Also in child_clean.R, inside each outer-batch iteration.
  • Assigns round-robin batch numbers to subjects in the already-filtered data.all: (seq_along(subjid.unique) - 1L) %% cores + 1L.
  • When parallel = FALSE (or a single-core auto-detect), cores = 1, making this a no-op: all subjects in the outer batch go to a single cleanchild() call.
  • When parallel = TRUE, dispatches via foreach::foreach(...) %dopar% to process inner batches in parallel across CPU cores.

The inner batching subdivides whatever data the outer wrapper provides into parallel work units. With parallel = FALSE, it has no effect. The adult algorithm has its own inner parallel batching system, structured identically.

Parallel processing

parallel = TRUE runs the inner batches concurrently. The worker processes are separate R sessions that resolve libraries from .libPaths() and need system.file() access to the inst/extdata/ reference tables. This means growthcleanr must be installed (via devtools::install_github(), devtools::install_local(), or CRAN), not merely source-loaded via devtools::load_all().

Practical note for developers: There is a limitation that applies only to package developers. Most uses of devtools — including devtools::install_github("growth-data-tools/growthcleanr", ...) and devtools::install_local(".") — actually install the package into your R library, and parallel = TRUE works normally after those calls. The issue only appears when a developer uses devtools::load_all() to load the source tree into the current R session without installing (a workflow used for rapid iteration on package code). The workaround in that case is to run devtools::install_local(".") once, which takes only a few seconds.

Results are bit-identical to sequential processing (verified on the 77,721-row syngrowth dataset). Typical observed speedups on 2,697 subjects with many errors (which results in longer run-time): ~114 s at parallel = FALSE, ~65 s at cores = 2 (1.7×), ~30 s at cores = 4 (3.9×).

Batch-invariant setup (the exclude.levels factor and the Tanner velocity reference) is performed once outside the outer loop so the cost is not repeated per batch; the WHO velocity tables are loaded per batch inside cleanchild().

Partial runs and preloaded references

Two mechanisms support workflows that call growthcleanr many times on overlapping data (simulation loops, error-injection pipelines, secure-environment workflows with updated data extracts): preloaded reference tables, and the gc_partial_run() wrapper for incremental re-cleans.

ref_tables + gc_preload_refs(). gc_preload_refs() reads the CDC and WHO growth-chart reference files once and returns a named list of closures (mtz_cdc_prelim and mtz_who_prelim). Passing that list as the ref_tables argument to subsequent cleangrowth() calls skips the per-call read_anthro() disk reads (≈0.9 seconds per call). The return value is a session-lifetime object; rebuild only if the reference files themselves change.

refs <- gc_preload_refs()
res  <- cleangrowth(..., ref_tables = refs)

gc_partial_run() — incremental re-cleans. When you re-clean a dataset that changed for only a subset of subjects, gc_partial_run() re-cleans just those subjects and reuses the earlier cleaned result for everyone else. This is correct because growthcleanr cleans each subject independently after reference recentering, so re-cleaning only the changed subjects yields exactly the rows those subjects would get in a full run; the combined result equals cleangrowth(new_data, ...).

baseline <- cleangrowth(old_data)
updated  <- gc_partial_run(new_data, baseline, changed_subjids = who_changed)

gc_partial_run() is a thin wrapper around cleangrowth(), not a mode of it: it slices new_data to the changed subjects (plus any subjects newly added relative to the cache; removed subjects are dropped), hands that subset to a single ordinary cleangrowth() call, and row-binds the retained cached rows to the fresh rows, ordered by id. Everything passed in ... — including checkpoint_dir, checkpoint_size, batch_size, ref_tables, and the output switches — is forwarded verbatim to that inner call, so a large changed subset can still be checkpointed. Because the cache never enters cleangrowth(), it cannot interact with the cleaning core.

Requirements: input must be long format; both new_data and cached_output must carry a per-row unique id (the stable key that links retained and fresh rows), and id values must be stable across runs; and ... must specify the same output options used to build cached_output — if the resulting columns differ, gc_partial_run() stops rather than silently produce NA-filled rows. See ?gc_partial_run for the full contract.

Because only the changed subjects are cleaned, the per-call cost scales with the fraction of subjects that changed: re-cleaning 5 % of subjects does roughly 5 % of the cleaning work of a full run (plus a small fixed cost to slice and merge). The savings are largest in loops where each iteration perturbs only a few subjects.

Checkpointed runs (the checkpoint / checkpoint_dir switch)

How the switch resolves. The pair checkpoint / checkpoint_dir is resolved once, before the checkpoint loop, into a concrete target. In priority order: a nested per-checkpoint call (.checkpoint_driven) never re-checkpoints; checkpoint = FALSE disables checkpointing and, if a checkpoint_dir was also passed, ignores it with a warning (the “nothing on disk” escape hatch is absolute); an explicit checkpoint_dir is honored as a persistent, resumable location (keep_checkpoints as given); and the default checkpoint = TRUE with no directory writes to an ephemeral file.path(tempdir(), "growthcleanr_checkpoints") with keep_checkpoints = FALSE and checkpoint_resume = FALSE, engaging only when the data exceeds one checkpoint (uniqueN(subjid) > checkpoint_size). A single checkpoint is the whole dataset cleaned in one in-memory pass and gives no benefit, so at or below one checkpoint’s worth of subjects the run stays fully in memory and writes nothing — which keeps the on-by-default behavior free for small and typical data. On a system whose temp dir is RAM-backed (e.g. Linux tmpfs), a very large dataset should pass a checkpoint_dir on a real disk. User-facing guidance is in vignette("large-datasets").

Whichever way it engages, the mechanics are the same. cleangrowth() splits subjects into checkpoints of checkpoint_size (default 5000, capped at 9999 checkpoints — a checkpoint_size that would exceed the cap is increased to stay within it, with a warning when you chose the size), cleans each checkpoint, and writes that checkpoint’s result to its own checkpoint_NNNN.rds file in the checkpoint directory before moving to the next. After the last checkpoint it combines all checkpoint files into a single result in the original input order. Reference tables are preloaded once (via gc_preload_refs()) and reused across checkpoints. Because subjects are independent, the checkpointed result is identical to cleaning the whole dataset at once — this includes wide / semi-wide input and output, which reshape once around the checkpoint loop (input is reshaped to long before checkpointing; the combined long result is re-widened once at the end).

Internally each checkpoint is cleaned by a nested cleangrowth(checkpoint_dir = NULL) call in long mode: the input funnel, date parsing, and id generation happen once in the outer call, so a checkpoint receives canonical long data with a valid unique id and every subject’s rows land in one checkpoint. Carry-through of extra non-growthcleanr columns works under checkpointing: the parked columns are reattached once to the combined result at the end, so a checkpointed run returns the same columns as a non-checkpointed one. Every subject is cleaned independently, so checkpointing never changes a result. The adult_cutpoint (clamped to [18, 20]) is finalized once in the outer call and forwarded to each checkpoint so every checkpoint uses the same value; growthcleanr does not change the cutpoint based on the data, so this is a dataset-independent constant. The all-adult advisory (which suggests adult_cutpoint = 18 when the data looks adult-only) and the consolidated input warning are each emitted once from the outer call over the whole dataset rather than per checkpoint.

checkpoint_size is the persist unit (one .rds per checkpoint) and is independent of batch_size, the in-memory unit within a checkpoint; batch_size < checkpoint_size is allowed, so a checkpoint sized for a reasonable number of resumable files can still be processed in smaller memory batches.

The per-checkpoint files exist for durability and resumability:

  • By default (checkpoint_resume = FALSE) a run starts fresh: any checkpoint files already in checkpoint_dir are deleted at the start, so the combined result contains only the current run’s checkpoints and a re-run never silently mixes in stale results from a different prior dataset.
  • With checkpoint_resume = TRUE, checkpoints that already have a checkpoint file are skipped, so an interrupted run resumes on only the unfinished checkpoints. Checkpoint membership is determined by the sorted set of subjects and checkpoint_size, so resuming requires the same dataset and checkpoint_size. It also requires the same other cleangrowth() arguments; these are not checked, and a mismatch silently mixes results from different settings.
  • keep_checkpoints (default TRUE) governs only whether the files are retained after a successful run; it is independent of checkpoint_resume, which governs start-of-run reuse.

cleangrowth_checkpoint() is a deprecated wrapper that forwards to cleangrowth(checkpoint_dir = ...) — its use_existing_checkpoint_results argument maps to checkpoint_resume — and warns on use; it will be removed in a future version. cleangrowth_checkpoint_combine() re-combines the saved checkpoint files without re-running the algorithm — useful if all checkpoints completed but the final combine step failed. It reads every checkpoint_NNNN.rds file in the directory. User-facing usage is in vignette("large-datasets").

Two unrelated uses of “checkpoint.” The checkpoint_data capture in Phase 12 of cleangrowth() is an internal z-score snapshot merged back onto the output for diagnostics; it is unrelated to checkpoint_dir and the checkpointed-run machinery that saves per-checkpoint result files to disk. The shared word is incidental.

Progress output

cleangrowth() reports progress at one of three levels, set by the quietly and verbose flags (both plain and checkpointed checkpoint_dir modes):

  • Silent (quietly = TRUE) — nothing is printed: no progress lines and no cleaning summary.
  • Minimal (the default) — a one-line cleaning in progress header (subject / measurement / unit counts), an X/Y counter as each memory batch or checkpoint finishes, and the end-of-run cleaning summary. A single-batch, non-checkpointed run therefore prints just the header and the summary.
  • Verbose (verbose = TRUE, which implies quietly = FALSE) — the detailed view: the milestone lines (preprocessing, cleaning child/cleaning adult, the per-batch BATCH i/n banner) plus granular per-step diagnostics (pre-filter and iteration counts for CF, EWMA, SDE, Evil twins; adult step headers). Intended for development and debugging.

The three nested processing units keep distinct, fixed names: checkpoint (checkpoint_size; used whenever a run has more than checkpoint_size subjects, unless checkpoint = FALSE), batch (batch_size, the in-memory split inside one cleangrowth() call), and parallel group (verbose only).

A minimal (default) checkpointed run — header, a per-checkpoint X/Y counter, then the summary:

[10:22:58] growthcleanr: cleaning in progress: 435,000 subjects, 1,740,000 measurements, 87 checkpoints of up to 5,000 subjects | checkpoint_dir: results/gc_ckpt

==================================================
  CHECKPOINT 1 / 87  |  5,000 subjects
==================================================
[10:23:36] checkpoint 1/87: done | 32s | elapsed 32s
...
[11:09:30] all 87 checkpoints complete | 435,000 subjects, 1,740,000 rows | total 46m32s
************************************************************
growthcleanr cleaning summary  (1,740,000 measurements)
  ...
************************************************************

At the verbose level each checkpoint additionally prints its preprocessing / cleaning child / cleaning adult milestone lines and the per-step diagnostics. A plain cleangrowth() call (no checkpoint_dir) prints the same header and summary; when batch_size forces more than one memory batch it adds a one-line batch i/n -- done counter at the minimal level (and the fuller BATCH i/n banner at verbose). Under a checkpointed run, each per-checkpoint cleangrowth() call is told its framing is owned by the checkpoint driver, so it stays quiet while the driver supplies the header, the per-checkpoint progress, and the total. When log_file is set, the full log is written there even under quietly = TRUE, so a colleague can monitor a run remotely.

Data Requirements and Input Format

Calling styles

cleangrowth() supports two calling styles:

  1. Data-frame style (primary). Pass a data.frame or data.table as the first argument (data). The six per-row arguments (subjid, param, agedays, sex, measurement, id) are then column-name strings, defaulting to the canonical names. Examples:

    cleangrowth(df)                                    # all defaults
cleangrowth(df, subjid = "patid", id = "row_id")   # remap two columns

  2. Vector style (legacy). Omit data; pass each field as a vector via named args, e.g. cleangrowth(subjid = df$subjid, param = df$param, ...). Retained for backward compatibility.

The data-frame path extracts vectors from data and merges into the vector path; both produce identical results.

Flexible sex and parameter coding

cleangrowth() accepts a range of sex and param codings so data from varied sources needs less pre-formatting, while guarding against silent miscoding. Both interpretations preserve the user’s verbatim submission (echoed back in the output sex / param columns); the interpreted values gc worked with are available as gc_internal_sex / gc_internal_param under internal_detail (or full_detail).

Sex. By default 0, "m", "b", "male", "boy" are read as male and 1, "f", "g", "female", "girl" as female — matched case-insensitively and whitespace-trimmed. Supply sex_coding to use your own codes; it is a named list whose male and female elements are the code vectors, and it replaces the defaults wholesale:

cleangrowth(df, sex_coding = list(male = c(0, "M", "boy"), female = c(1, "F", "girl")))

Handling of the interpreted sex:

  • Recognized codes clean normally.
  • Missing (NA/blank) and present-but-unrecognized codes on pediatric rows are set aside as Exclude-Missing-Info, contributing an “unrecognized sex” bullet (which names the offending values and leads with the sex_coding fix) to the consolidated input warning, so a coding gc did not expect is visible, not silent. Pediatric measurements are cleaned only with a recognized sex value (the child z-scores are sex-specific). If no pediatric row has a usable value in the sex column and there are no adult rows, the run stops, since nothing could be cleaned. If there are adult rows, the run continues: the pediatric rows are set aside and the bullet says that this is every pediatric measurement and asks you to check the sex column mapping. In either case, when every pediatric row is at least 18 years old, the message also suggests adult_cutpoint = 18 so all values are cleaned with the adult algorithm.
  • Adult rows. A sex column is always required, but the sex column value may be blank or NA for adults (ages at or above adult_cutpoint): the adult algorithm does not require a valid value in the sex column, but when available, it is used in the Evil Twins step and in calculating whether a value falls in the unit error range.
  • The 1=male/2=female trap. growthcleanr reads 1 as female. A column coded 1=male/2=female would therefore misclassify every male as female while only the 2s drop out — a plausible-looking wrong answer. So when the default coding is in use and every present sex value is 1 or 2 (with at least one 2), cleangrowth() hard-stops and tells the user to recode or to declare the coding with sex_coding = list(male = 1, female = 2). Passing an explicit sex_coding suppresses the guard. The guard is checked once on the whole dataset, so under checkpointing it stops before the first checkpoint is cleaned, however the data are sorted. A column with pediatric rows and more than one subject in which every value is 1 has no 0 or 2 to reveal the coding and could be single-sex data under either scheme, so it is not stopped: it is read as female with a prominent warning, which an explicit sex_coding also removes.

Parameter. growthcleanr recognizes only the spelled-out canonical tokens — WEIGHTKG, WEIGHTLBS, HEIGHTCM, HEIGHTIN, LENGTHCM, LENGTHIN, HEADCM, HEADIN — matched case-insensitively and whitespace-trimmed. There are deliberately no built-in abbreviations: a short label such as WT, HT, or HC is not assumed to be a growthcleanr parameter, because it just as easily names something that is not a body measurement (a statistical sample weight, for instance). To have a non-canonical label recognized, declare it with param_coding. The imperial tokens convert at 2.54 cm/in (HEIGHTIN → HEIGHTCM, LENGTHIN → LENGTHCM, HEADIN → HEADCM) or 2.2046226 lb/kg (WEIGHTLBS → WEIGHTKG).

Supply param_coding to map your own labels. A remapped label defaults to its metric target; to declare that a column is imperial, route it to an imperial parameter:

# route two custom labels; treat a "WEIGHT" column as pounds and "HT"/"STATURE" as cm
cleangrowth(df, param_coding = list(WEIGHTLBS = "WEIGHT", HEIGHTCM = c("HT", "STATURE")))

It is a named list keyed by canonical parameter. A name that is not a canonical parameter, or one label mapped to two parameters, is an error. Params matching nothing are set aside as Exclude-Not-GC-Param (a bullet in the consolidated input warning, never a stop — extracts legitimately carry labs and vitals).

Systematic unit-error warning. After cleaning, if more than 20% of a parameter’s cleaned values fall in the unit-error range (unit_error_range; magnitudes consistent with a metric/imperial mix-up), cleangrowth() emits a soft warning() — a large share suggests the whole column is in the wrong unit (e.g. weight recorded in pounds but labeled WEIGHTKG, or a column mapped to a metric target that was actually imperial). Fix by labeling the column with the imperial parameter or mapping it via param_coding.

Input format: long, semi-wide, and wide

The input_format argument selects the shape of data:

  • "long" (default) — one row per measurement, the classic format described above.
  • "semi_wide" — one row per visit: a subjid, an age source, a sex, and one column per parameter (at most one value per parameter per visit).
  • "wide" — one row per subject: a subjid, a sex, and repeated observation blocks marked by a _N column suffix (agedays_1, wt_1, ht_1, agedays_2, wt_2, …).

Semi-wide and wide both require the data-frame style, and both are reshaped to canonical long form before any cleaning, so results are identical to submitting the same measurements in long format. Results come back in the same shape by default (output_format mirrors input_format); see Output format: semi-wide and Output format: wide below. Set output_format = "long" for the full per-measurement result table, which merges back onto the source data by subjid/param/agedays.

The format is never auto-detected: input_format defaults to "long", so semi-wide or wide data submitted without setting it is not silently mis-cleaned — it fails, because long format requires param/measurement columns (and a single agedays column) that reshaped data lack. When the columns look reshaped, the error names input_format as the likely fix.

Parameter value columns are mapped with semiwide_cols, a named list of gc-parameter → column name. If omitted, columns literally named as recognized parameters (WEIGHTKG, HEIGHTCM, LENGTHCM, HEADCM, WEIGHTLBS, HEIGHTIN, LENGTHIN, HEADIN) are used:

# columns already named WEIGHTKG / HEIGHTCM / HEADCM
cleangrowth(visits, input_format = "semi_wide")

# custom value-column names
cleangrowth(visits, input_format = "semi_wide",
            semiwide_cols = list(WEIGHTKG = "wt_kg", HEIGHTCM = "ht_cm", HEADCM = "head_cm"))

Structural columns reuse the usual remap arguments (subjid, sex, and either an agedays column or dob + visit_date columns, from which agedays is computed). Behavior details:

  • Empty cells vs. zeros. An NA cell means “no measurement of that parameter at this visit” and is dropped during reshape (no output row). A literal 0 is not an empty cell: exactly as in long format, its value is returned unchanged in measurement and the row is flagged Exclude-Missing-Info (growthcleanr treats 0 as missing for cleaning purposes but never alters the value it hands back). Do not pad absent measurements with 0 — use an empty/NA cell.
  • At least one recognized parameter column must be present (otherwise an error). A missing weight or height/length column warns; a missing head-circumference column warns only when the data include any visit under 2 years of age.
  • Length vs height is a long-format-only feature. Semi-wide input always uses default handling of linear measurements (values under 2 years are treated as recumbent length, values 2 years and over as standing height, using estimated corrected age for children whose data are consistent with prematurity or small-for-gestational age (SGA) and who receive an assigned gestational age for cleaning purposes), so length.adjust = TRUE is rejected. A LENGTHCM/LENGTHIN column is accepted at any age and gets default handling, giving the same result as mapping it to HEIGHTCM/HEIGHTIN; the adult algorithm ignores the length/height label entirely. To use the two-directional length.adjust reconciliation, submit the data in long format.
  • Duplicate column names are an error. If a subjid, sex, age, or parameter column name appears more than once, growthcleanr stops. R’s column indexing silently keeps only the first such column, so cleaning would proceed on a dataset with a shadowed, dropped column — rename or drop the duplicate instead. (An unmapped extra column is simply ignored: parameters come from the column you map, not from any value.)
  • Same-day duplicates. Because a visit row holds at most one value per parameter, two measurements of the same parameter on the same day must appear as two rows sharing the same (subjid, agedays). growthcleanr keeps one and flags the other as a same-day extraneous value, exactly as for long input. Each parameter is handled independently (weight/height pairing across same-day rows is not preserved).
  • Per-measurement ids / same-day tiebreaking. The reshape mints deterministic per-measurement ids in a stable, documented emission order (subject in first-appearance order; within a subject by visit, then by parameter in weight → height/length → head-circumference order). If you supply an id (the id argument, or a column named id), a subject’s visit rows are ordered by your id first (sorted by value, so character ids sort alphabetically) and by input row second; the id need not be unique. The same input always produces the same result, but which of two same-day duplicates is flagged can depend on this emission order. To control same-day tiebreaking, give same-day visit rows ids in the order you want (a higher id is preferred, except at birth), or reformat to long format and set a per-measurement id yourself.
  • Ids in long output. With output_format = "long", each input row becomes one output row per measurement, so a row id cannot identify a single measurement. growthcleanr returns its own per-measurement number as gc_internal_id, and your id (the id argument, or a column named id) under your own column name, repeated on each measurement from that input row. With no id column there is no id column in the output. Your other columns are returned too (carry_through), repeated on each measurement from their row. A column with your name always holds only your own values: if your id or another column has the name of a column growthcleanr returns (e.g. exclude or param), it comes back as userinput_<name>, with a warning.
  • Column names in long output.
